Cunning, as a noun, means the quality of being clever in a sly, sneaky, or deceptive way to get what you want — especially when others don't notice what you're really doing.

It is not just being smart. It is being smart in a crafty, indirect, and often self-serving way.

Think of it this way: a mathematician who solves a hard equation is intelligent. But a person who tricks their opponent into making a mistake they never saw coming — that person has cunning.
What Makes Cunning Special (and Different from Just "Cleverness")

Cunning has three key ingredients that set it apart from ordinary intelligence:

1. Cleverness with a hidden purpose.
A cunning person thinks several steps ahead and hides their true intentions. On the surface, they may appear harmless, cooperative, or even simple — but underneath, they are carefully working toward their own goal.

2. Indirectness.
A cunning person rarely goes straight at a target. They find ways around obstacles — through tricks, misdirection, manipulation, or careful timing. They achieve things by making others do what they want, often without those others even realising it.

3. The ability to exploit weaknesses.
Cunning involves reading people and situations sharply — noticing vulnerabilities, gaps, and opportunities — and using them to one's advantage.

Cunning sits in a morally grey zone.

It is not an openly admirable quality like courage or honesty. When you say someone has cunning, there is an edge to it — a suggestion that their cleverness is a little unsettling, a little dangerous, perhaps untrustworthy. It is the kind of cleverness that makes you watch your back.

However, it is also not purely evil. Cunning can be used for survival, for justice, or for protecting oneself in a world where raw strength isn't enough. A weak person outwitting a powerful bully with cunning earns a kind of grudging respect.

So the word can carry:

  • Admiration — "Impressive. I never saw that coming."
  • Suspicion — "Watch out. This person cannot be trusted."
  • A mix of both — which is where cunning most naturally lives.
Real-World Examples to Make It Click

The Fox:
In literature and folklore across many cultures, the fox is the symbol of cunning. It doesn't win by being the strongest or the fastest. It wins by being sly — by outsmarting hunters, avoiding traps, and finding angles others didn't think of. That is cunning perfectly embodied.

The Chess Player:
Imagine a chess player who deliberately makes a move that looks like a mistake — sacrificing a piece. Their opponent, thinking they've spotted a weakness, pounces on it. But that was the trap all along. The "mistake" was bait. That kind of deceptive, long-planned cleverness is cunning.

The Politician:
A politician who chooses their words so carefully that they technically never lie — but consistently lead people to believe something false — is using cunning. They are clever enough to deceive without being caught in a direct lie.

The Villain in a Story:
Most memorable villains in fiction don't win through brute force. They win through cunning — elaborate plans, manipulation of allies, exploitation of heroes' emotions, traps laid weeks in advance. Their cunning is what makes them genuinely threatening.

• "The general won the battle not through superior numbers, but through cunning."
  • "She had the cunning of someone who had survived decades of office politics."
  • "The escape required both courage and cunning."
  • "His opponents underestimated him — a mistake, because his cunning was extraordinary."

Cunning exists on a spectrum:

  • Mild cunning looks like street-smartness — knowing how to navigate tricky social situations cleverly.
  • Strong cunning looks like masterful manipulation — orchestrating events from the shadows so that everything falls exactly as planned, with no one the wiser.

The stronger the cunning, the more unsettling — and impressive — it tends to feel.

These words are close cousins of cunning and will help sharpen your understanding:

  • Guile — very similar to cunning; deceptive cleverness, but with a slightly more literary feel.
  • Craftiness — another near-synonym; the quality of being crafty or scheming.
  • Slyness — clever in a secretive, sneaky way.
  • Wiliness — the quality of being wily (tricky and full of schemes, like a wily coyote).
  • Shrewdness — similar, but slightly more neutral; sharp judgement and cleverness (can be without deception).
  • Deviousness — more overtly negative; going through indirect, dishonest routes.

Among these, cunning is the most powerful and versatile, and carries the deepest mix of reluctant respect and wariness.
Cunning is the quality of using clever, indirect, and often deceptive thinking to achieve your goals — a trait that is as unsettling as it is impressive.
